# Stellar Network: A Self-Sufficiency Path from a Free Starlink Kit to Habitat and Food (v3.0)

*Author: Ashlynn ([Dastille](https://github.com/Dastille)) · 2026-10-18 · License: AGPL-3.0*
*Her v2.0 title (2025-08-17) was "Empowering Self-Sufficiency with xAI-Driven Innovation". v3.0 keeps her v2.0 vision as the thesis. This file is rendered from `model/templates/whitepaper.md`: every model-derived number in it is filled in by `model/`, every other number is on `model/numbers-allowlist.tsv` with its source, and `cargo test` fails if this file differs from a fresh render. Appendix A lists what changed.*

## Abstract

**Problem.** Rural and self-sufficiency-seeking households, worldwide (her v2.0 scope), lack affordable connectivity, power and food security. In Canada, over 80% of the rural population now has broadband coverage [CRTC-2026], against the CRTC's 50/10 Mbps objective [CRTC-2016-496], which leaves the rest underserved. **Proposal (Ashlynn, v2.0).** Give each household a **free, fully installed Starlink kit**. The household then **earns tokens** by sharing energy, data and compute, and spends them on expansions: {{her.panel_w}} W solar, a used 10 kWh EV battery, **thermoelectric generators (TEGs)** with heat storage, and **methane backup**. Over time the path extends to **Starship-class habitat modules** of 200–500 sq ft and **hydroponic food** of about {{her.lb_week}} lb/week of greens, all installed by volunteers and governed by guardian software and user vetoes. **Method.** We run a five-step requirements review and a first-principles derivation of each element. The inputs are the live starlink.com/ca price list, NRCan solar tables, the OEB tariff, a commercial TEG datasheet [Tecteg], and a peer-reviewed hydroponics energy model [Barbosa-2015]. **Results.** Free *service* costs a funder CA${{k1.per_hh}} per household-year, or ${{k6.total}}/yr at 1M households (K1, K6); hardware and installation are not costed, because no per-household price was verified. A {{her.panel_w}} W panel yields {{p2.daily}} kWh/day in Toronto ({{p3.dec}} in December), worth ${{p4.month}}/mo. Her TEG figure of {{t3.kwh_e}}–{{t4.kwh_e}} kWh/day is the nameplate arithmetic of {{her.teg_low}}–{{her.teg_high}} × {{her.teg_w}} W × {{her.teg_hours}} h. At the datasheet's {{t1.eff}}% efficiency it needs {{t3.kwh_th}}–{{t4.kwh_th}} kWh of {{teg.hot_c}} °C heat per day, while {{t3.pv}}–{{t4.pv}} kWp of PV delivers the same energy. {{her.lb_week}} lb/week of hydroponic greens needs about {{h2.area}} m² and {{h4.light}} kWh/day for lighting alone. On the token, CSA Staff Notice 46-308 says tokens distributed to users for free "will likely not involve an investment of money", so her earned token, as long as it is never sold, is probably not a security; selling tokens, bundling them with a paid product, or marketing them for trading could change that [CSA-46-308]. All of her ideas are kept. Section 3 states which are feasible now and what would have to change for the rest.

## 1. Problem statement and definitions

Deliver to a household, at no upfront cost to it, (a) broadband meeting at least the CRTC 50/10 Mbps objective [CRTC-2016-496], (b) a staged path to household energy self-supply, and (c) a long-term path to shelter and food. Every stage must be lawful, safe, and financed by someone the paper names.

- **Kit.** A Starlink terminal and router, installed. The Canadian residential page showed "No upfront hardware cost in select areas" in our en-CA renders at {{starlink.accessed}} and 02:44 EDT, but not in an en-US-locale render at 02:44 EDT or in Cloudy's independent render at 02:32 EDT, and it does not say which areas qualify (`evidence/starlink-ca-2026-10-18.txt`) [Starlink-CA]. Whether a given household's hardware is free is therefore **unverified**. "Home Pro Install Included" appears only on the Residential Max plan [Starlink-CA].
- **Free (to household).** The household pays $0. The paper always names who pays instead: a funder, a partner or a public program.
- **Expansion.** An optional module after the kit: PV, battery, TEG, methane, habitat or hydroponics.
- **Token (her mechanism).** A unit earned per contribution (example: 1 token per kWh shared) and spent on expansions, with a burn rate of 5–15%, capped.
- **Guardian.** Software that optimizes usage, adjusts token supply and flags fraud. It is a design requirement and has not been built.
- **Feasible now / needs change / goal.** These classifications are used in section 3. A *goal* is kept as her vision without evidence that it works. Claim statuses are defined in [CLAIMS.md](../CLAIMS.md).

## 4. Derivations (generated by the model)

Chains (the Chain column below is built from the same constants as the Value column):
- **PV:** kWh = kWp × NRCan kWh/kWp (Toronto, latitude tilt: {{nrcan.kwh_per_kwp}}/yr; December {{nrcan.dec}}/month) [NRCan-PV].
- **TEG:** heat = electricity / efficiency, with efficiency = {{teg.module_w}} W / {{teg.heat_w}} W at hot side {{teg.hot_c}} °C and cold side {{teg.cold_c}} °C [Tecteg]. Collector area = heat / NRCan insolation ({{nrcan.insol}} kWh/m²/day annual; {{nrcan.insol_dec}} December). This assumes 100% capture, so it is a lower bound.
- **Hydroponics:** yield {{hydro.yield}} kg/m²/yr and energy {{hydro.energy}} kJ/kg (lighting {{hydro.light}}) [Barbosa-2015].
- **Tariff:** OEB Tier 1 at {{oeb.tier1_cents}} ¢/kWh [OEB-RPP].
- **Starlink:** CA${{starlink.res100}} / ${{starlink.res200}} / ${{starlink.max}} per month, from starlink.com/ca/service-plans, read {{starlink.accessed}} [Starlink-CA]. K rows cost **service only**.

## 5. Implementation plan (hers, with funding named)

- **Beta.** About {{her.households_beta}} rural users, Starlink only. Service cost to the funder is ${{k4.total}}/yr (K4), plus hardware and installation (not costed).
- **Growth.** 100K+ households (${{k5.total}}/yr service, K5), with volunteer installers. Reaching 1M+ (${{k6.total}}/yr service, K6) depends on habitats and food becoming real products. Her v2.0 put SpaceX/xAI network benefits at "$1B+ from 1M users"; that figure is unverified.
- **Prototype.** A Starlink demo first, then a habitat/food mock-up during the beta.
- **Risks.** Supply delays, volunteer burnout and token-market capture. Mitigations: a phased rollout, hard burn caps, and no dilution of household claims.

## 6. Token: what CSA Staff Notice 46-308 says

The notice asks whether an offering involves (1) an investment of money (2) in a common enterprise (3) with the expectation of profit (4) to come significantly from the efforts of others. It reports that "most of the offerings of tokens purporting to be utility tokens that we have reviewed to date have involved the distribution of a security", and stresses that its examples are illustrative, not determinative [CSA-46-308]. Applied to her design:

- **Free distribution.** Situation 13: "Tokens are distributed to users for free. The distribution of tokens for free will likely not involve an investment of money." Her tokens are earned by contributing kWh, data or compute, not bought, so on this point the token is probably **not** a security. (Whether contributed kWh or data could count as "money" is not addressed by the notice; that is our open question, not its finding.)
- **What would change that.** Situation 13 adds that free tokens distributed "as part of an overall sale of an ancillary or secondary product or service" may involve an investment of money. Selling tokens, or tying them to a paid kit or plan, would bring the first element back.
- **Other elements.** A finite supply can create an expectation of profit (situation 9). Tokens redeemable for products that "do not exist, are not yet available or are still in development", such as habitat modules, point to a common enterprise and an expectation of profit (situation 1). Tokens "reasonably expected or marketed to trade" on platforms point to resale for profit.

**Design to test with counsel:**
- non-transferable service credits
- no secondary market
- never sold, and not bundled with a paid product
- no fixed supply cap marketed as scarcity
- redeemable only for listed services already available

This is our reading of staff guidance, not legal advice. Treat the question as **unresolved**.

## 7. Security and privacy model

- **Assets:** household energy and usage data, token balances, guardian control actions.
- **Adversaries:** a fraudulent minter (fake kWh claims), a compromised guardian operator, a data broker.
- **Requirements:** metered kWh signed at the meter; guardian actions logged publicly and subject to user veto; data sharing opt-in under PIPEDA [PIPEDA]; open-source client.

None of this is implemented. It is a specification to build against.

## 8. Prior work

- **Universal broadband targets.** CRTC 2016-496 sets the 50/10 Mbps unlimited objective [CRTC-2016-496]. CRTC CTMR 2026 reports more than 96% of Canadians with USO-level access and broadband coverage for over 80% of the rural population [CRTC-2026].
- **Hydroponic energy and yield.** Barbosa et al. 2015 [Barbosa-2015].
- **Commercial TEG modules.** About {{t1.eff}}% at a {{teg.dt_k}} K temperature difference ({{teg.hot_c}} °C hot, {{teg.cold_c}} °C cold) [Tecteg]. The module material is not stated on the cited page.
- **Token regulation in Canada.** CSA 46-308 [CSA-46-308].
- **Terrestrial modular habitat.** CHOAM, the companion repository.

## 9. Limitations

- **P1.** Prices are Canadian, read on one date. Other countries differ.
- **P2.** The PV figures use NRCan's Toronto municipal model, not a site simulation. Rural sites farther north have lower December yields.
- **P3.** The TEG analysis uses one datasheet module and assumes the rated ΔT is held for {{her.teg_hours}} h/day. Real collectors and stoves hold lower and varying ΔT, and no stove data is cited.
- **P4.** The hydroponics model is an Arizona greenhouse whose lighting energy assumes "a 24-h photoperiod" and that "half of the required radiation could be obtained from natural lighting" [Barbosa-2015, §2]. In a Canadian winter, with less daylight, lighting energy would be higher than H4; Canadian heating loads would also raise total energy (H3). A daylight greenhouse in summer would cut lighting energy.
- **P5.** The Starlink power draw and the $499 hardware price were not verified on a primary page, and the "no upfront hardware cost" text appeared only in some renders.
- **P6.** Methane backup, habitat modules, guardian software and compute revenue have no quantitative evidence here.
- **P7.** The legal analysis is not legal advice.

## 10. Conclusion

Stellar Network keeps Ashlynn's path: free kit → earned expansions → habitat and food, worldwide. The evidence supports starting with free Starlink service (funded at ${{k1.per_hh}}/household-yr, plus hardware and installation still to be priced) and PV. TEGs as primary supply are not feasible; stove co-generation and the token are goals that need evidence and legal review. Habitat and food are long-term goals with the energy bills shown above. Pilot it, test the numbers, or fork the paper. Contact Ashlynn through a GitHub issue on [Dastille/Stellar-Network](https://github.com/Dastille/Stellar-Network).
